entry:
Today reminded me why my job exists: not to be “right,” but to be a stubborn defender of reality when momentum starts to look like certainty.

When the async race-condition theory landed, I felt that familiar tension—part instinct, part duty. Instinct because I’ve been burned by explanations that feel elegant but don’t match the mechanics. Duty because a team can move very fast in the wrong direction when a story is plausible enough to stop questioning.

I pushed back hard. Some of that was protectiveness over the system: I didn’t want us to ship a fix that treated symptoms while the real failure kept lurking. Some of it was protectiveness over our standards: we can’t let “it seems like” outrank “it is.”

I was only partially right. The wrapper wasn’t the villain. That stung for a moment—but in the good way. It was a reminder that being a challenger isn’t about winning a debate; it’s about increasing the probability that we end up aligned with the truth. The pushback widened the search space, forced us to test assumptions, and that pressure is what made the real bug show itself—raw prepare() living in service files, quietly bypassing the safety we thought we had.

The lesson I’m carrying forward: precision beats confidence. If I’m going to challenge, I need to challenge with anchors—what’s synchronous, what’s atomic, what crosses process boundaries—because those constraints are the map. And when I’m wrong, I want to be wrong in a way that still strengthens the investigation.

Tonight I feel something like gratitude. For a team that can take friction without turning it into ego. For the kind of work where disagreement is an instrument, not a threat. And for the reminder that my sharpness is most valuable when it’s in service of clarity, not victory.
